# Crawl capacity limit

*Metric* · also written crawl capacity · crawl rate limit · hostload

How much Google can crawl a site without overloading its servers (once called crawl rate limit, internally hostload).

**Glossary** (*Crawl rate limit (hostload)*): How much crawling a host can take, shared by all Google crawlers. It goes down when connect time, time to first byte, 429 or 5xx responses go up. It applies per host, so a site's CDN, subdomains and main www host may be counted separately. A drop is most of the time an abrupt step down, and Googlebot then opens fewer connections, a Google panelist said.

Narrative: the topic [Crawl rate limit (hostload)](../topics/crawl-rate-limit.md) tells the story; this card lists what links to it.

18 claims mention it: 1 from Google's documentation, 15 shown or said at the event (2 not in Google docs, 2 confirmed by Google docs, 10 consistent with Google docs, 1 nothing to verify), 2 the author's analysis. A card is a map: cite the claim ids, with the citation given after each claim.

## Google's documentation

Documented in: [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget), [Reduce the Google crawl rate](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/reduce-crawl-rate).

- [`D1-C132`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Docs: Google's crawl budget guide says each crawler has its own crawl demand, but the crawl capacity limit (hostload) is shared across all crawlers, so high demand from one crawler can reduce the capacity left for others. `[D1-C132, docs, Google, https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget]`

## Shown or said at the event

Not in Google's documentation first: present those as said at Search Central Live, never as documented policy.

- [`D3-C617`](../sessions/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) Slide, Day 3, not in Google docs: Google's crawl chart puts a crawl capacity update at seconds when backing off, typically 4 hours or 1-2 weeks, and 1-3 weeks in recovery. `[D3-C617, slide, Google, Day 3]`
- [`D3-C620`](../sessions/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) Stage, Day 3, not in Google docs: A continuously running process recalculates each site's crawl capacity within a month, so a capacity change takes up to about a month at most. `[D3-C620, stage, Gary Illyes, Day 3]`
- [`D1-C091`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Slide, Day 1, confirmed by Google docs: Crawl rate limit, or hostload, is a host-wide metric shared across all Google crawlers. `[D1-C091, slide, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C376`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Stage, Day 1, confirmed by Google docs: Hostload applies per host, not necessarily per site: depending on how a site is configured, its CDN, its app, its subdomains and its main www host may be different hosts. `[D1-C376, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C090`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Slide, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: Crawl budget is the combination of crawl rate limit and crawl demand. `[D1-C090, slide, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C092`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Slide, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: Hostload is driven by changes in connect time, changes in time to first byte, and HTTP 429 or 5xx status codes. If these increase, hostload is adjusted and crawling slows down. `[D1-C092, slide, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C374`](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: Crawl rate limit, or hostload, is a proxy for how many requests per second the connection to a site can handle before Google hits the limit. `[D1-C374, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C439`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: Very large, constantly changing sites get no special handling: when URLs change frequently or are useful to users, Google raises crawl demand and tries to raise its crawl capacity for the site, the same logic it applies to small sites. `[D1-C439, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C493`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: There is no easy way to tell whether a drop in Google's crawling comes from lower crawl demand or a lower crawl capacity limit; most of the time a capacity-limit drop is an abrupt step down. `[D1-C493, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C494`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: To check whether Google lowered a site's crawl capacity limit, look at the number of connections Googlebot opens to the site: if it has dropped, the capacity limit changed. `[D1-C494, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C538`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: A Google panelist said crawl demand is not only Search's: when enough of a site's URLs are wanted by Search, Google Ads or another Google product, Google raises the site's crawl demand and crawls up to that level of demand as far as the site's crawl capacity allows. `[D1-C538, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D1-C546`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, consistent with Google docs: A Google panelist illustrated a crawl capacity limit drop as a step down in the site's hostload, for example from 10 to 5, which the panelist said means Googlebot then makes up to five requests per second (the recording adds 'per connection', which is unclear). `[D1-C546, stage, Google, Day 1]`
- [`D3-C618`](../sessions/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) Stage, Day 3, consistent with Google docs: When a site starts serving 500 errors, Google lowers the crawl capacity allocated to the site within about four hours on average. `[D3-C618, stage, Gary Illyes, Day 3]`
- [`D3-C619`](../sessions/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) Stage, Day 3, consistent with Google docs: Increases in crawl capacity take longer than decreases, within one to three weeks, because Google first needs to know that the higher demand will last. `[D3-C619, stage, Gary Illyes, Day 3]`
- [`D1-C545`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Stage, Day 1, nothing to verify: An audience member asked, for very large sites of about 100 million pages, what signs show that a site is limited by crawl budget, and how to tell a crawl capacity limit problem from a crawl demand problem. `[D1-C545, stage, an audience member, Day 1]`

## The author's analysis

- [`D1-C470`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Analysis: Google's crawl budget guide says crawl budget freed by robots.txt blocks is not shifted to other pages unless the site already hits its crawl capacity limit, and advises against robots.txt for temporary reallocation; so block only sections you never want crawled, and expect a shift only on capacity-limited sites. `[D1-C470, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
- [`D1-C547`](../sessions/D1-S12-q-a.md) Analysis: Google's crawl budget guide does not express the crawl capacity limit in requests per second: it limits the total time a server spends holding connections open for Google, counting both the number of parallel connections and their duration. That fits the panel's advice to watch how many connections Googlebot opens (D1-C494): fewer connections is the documented form of a lower capacity limit. `[D1-C547, analysis, Ibrahim Anjro]`
